meta.name: Data Centers
meta.definition: The data center industry comprises facilities (hyperscale, colocation, enterprise and edge) that house servers, storage, networking and power/cooling infrastructure to run cloud, AI, telecom and enterprise computing workloads, including the construction, equipment and operating ecosystem around them.

summary.headline: India's data centre market is valued at roughly USD 9.8 billion in 2025 and capacity has crossed about 1.6-1.9 GW by mid-2026, but India still holds only ~2-5% of global capacity despite generating ~20% of the world's data - setting up a multi-decade build-out toward 6-9 GW by 2029-30 backed by over USD 120 billion of hyperscaler and conglomerate commitments.
key_takeaways: India's installed data centre IT capacity roughly tripled from ~520 MW (2020) to ~1.5-1.9 GW by FY26, and multiple trackers (JLL, CBRE, Jefferies) project 4-9+ GW by 2029-30 on the back of AI, cloud and data-localisation demand.

Mumbai (and Navi Mumbai) dominates with roughly half of India's capacity, followed by Chennai, Hyderabad, Bengaluru and Delhi-NCR; the top 5-6 colocation operators (CtrlS, NTT, STT GDC, Nxtra, Sify, Adani Connex) control ~65-90% of installed capacity.

India is heavily import-dependent for servers, GPUs, storage and power/cooling equipment (60-70% of high-value components imported), and the rupee, global chip supply and US-China tech tensions directly affect project costs and timelines.

Government policy is now a major tailwind: infrastructure status for 5MW+ data centres, a 20-year tax holiday for foreign cloud providers (Budget 2026-27, valid till 2047), the IndiaAI Mission's subsidised GPU access, and state-level land/power incentives (Maharashtra, Telangana, Tamil Nadu, UP, Karnataka, Gujarat, Rajasthan) are accelerating investment.

Despite the boom, India's power costs, grid-connection delays, water stress in cluster states, and reliance on diesel/import-heavy equipment remain key constraints; EBITDA margins for established operators are a healthy 40-55% but capex per MW (~Rs 50-70 crore) keeps the business capital-intensive and debt-heavy (D/E often ~1.0).
summary.report_markdown:
## Market size and trajectory
India's data centre market is valued at roughly **USD 9.79 billion in 2025** (Arizton/MarkNtel), though estimates vary widely by scope - from USD 4-10 billion depending on whether construction, IT hardware, colocation revenue or EBITDA-based valuation is used. ANAROCK estimates the industry's EBITDA-based enterprise value at **USD 10 billion** (31 March 2024, 20x EV/EBITDA), with FY24 industry revenue of USD 2.4 billion and debt of USD 1.2 billion. KPMG (July 2026) pegs India's market at **~USD1.7 billion in FY26 rising to ~USD6.8 billion by FY30** (INR14k crore to INR61k crore), implying India's share of the global data-centre market doubling from 2-3% to ~5% over that period.

On capacity, trackers disagree on the exact number but agree on direction: CEEW/PIB cite installed capacity growing from **~375-520 MW in 2020 to ~1.5-1.9 GW by 2025-26**; JLL puts India at **1.6 GW in mid-2026**, tripling to **6 GW by 2029**; Jefferies is more bullish at **~8-9.2 GW by 2030**; CareEdge projects **~4 GW by FY30** needing ~Rs 1.5 lakh crore of capex (plus Rs 3-4 lakh crore more if tenant IT-equipment spend is included).

## Growth drivers
- **AI and hyperscale build-out**: AI/ML workloads are 5-10x more power-intensive than traditional cloud; rack densities are rising from 8-12 kW to 40-150 kW, pushing capex and liquid-cooling adoption.
- **Data localisation**: The Digital Personal Data Protection Act (DPDP) 2023, RBI payment-data rules and sector mandates are driving on-shoring of data that was previously hosted offshore (Singapore/Ireland), expected to add 1,800-2,000 MW of demand by 2027.
- **Cloud, 5G and digital payments**: India's internet base crossed ~1 billion, UPI processes 18-20+ billion transactions/month, and 5G subscriptions are set to rise ~8x by 2030 - all compounding data creation and compute demand.
- **Policy support**: Infrastructure status (2022), a 20-year tax holiday for foreign cloud providers (Budget 2026-27, to 2047), IndiaAI Mission's subsidised GPU access (34,000+ GPUs onboarded), and state-level incentives (land subsidies, stamp-duty and electricity-duty exemptions) in Maharashtra, Telangana, Tamil Nadu, UP, Karnataka, Gujarat, Rajasthan, Odisha, Haryana and Andhra Pradesh.
- **Lower build costs**: Mumbai is rated the world's 2nd-cheapest data-centre construction location (~US$7/watt vs US$10/W in the US), and India's capex is ~30-45% cheaper than China/US, though still requiring large upfront investment.

## Headwinds and risks for an India investor
- **Import dependence**: 60-70% of high-value DC components (servers, GPUs, storage, cooling, transformers) are imported; a 2% INR depreciation can lift landed server costs by ~1.6% given an ~80% import share of server bill-of-materials. India also lacks domestic HDD, NAND flash and liquid-cooling manufacturing.
- **Power and grid constraints**: Power is 65-75% of operating cost; India's T&D losses (16.6%) are more than double the global average, grid-connection queues run 18-36 months in Mumbai/Maharashtra, and per-million-internet-user DC capacity (~1 MW) lags China (4 MW), EU (12 MW) and the US (51 MW).
- **Water stress**: Clusters are concentrated in Maharashtra, Telangana and Tamil Nadu - states already under severe water stress; a 100 MW hyperscale facility can use ~2 million litres/day.
- **Geopolitical/China dumping risk is limited here but global chip supply (HBM, GPUs) remains concentrated with a handful of makers, and US export controls on advanced AI chips affect India's AI-DC buildout timelines.
- **Capital intensity and leverage**: Capex of Rs 50-70 crore/MW, 70-80% debt funding typical, and interest-cover of only 2-3x for the sector, though infrastructure-status financing (15-20 year tenor, 8.5-10.5%) is improving terms.

## Competitive landscape
The market is moderately concentrated: the top 5 colocation operators (CtrlS, NTT, STT GDC, Nxtra by Airtel, Sify, Adani Connex) together hold roughly 65-90% of installed capacity depending on the measure used, though new entrants (Reliance, AirTrunk, CapitaLand, Equinix, hyperscalers self-building) are expected to dilute this to ~70-75% by FY31. Mumbai/Navi Mumbai and Chennai together account for 70-80% of capacity; emerging hubs include Hyderabad, Delhi-NCR, Pune, Bengaluru and newer locations like Visakhapatnam, Kolkata and GIFT City.

## Outlook
India is positioned to be one of APAC's fastest-growing DC markets (CAGR estimates 13.6-24.6% depending on scope) through 2030-35, but remains a demand-led, capital-import-heavy build-out story rather than a domestic-manufacturing-led one - making policy execution (grid upgrades, PLI-driven local hardware assembly, water-sensitive siting) central to whether India can move from ~2-5% of global capacity today toward the 10-12 GW target floated for 2030.

sections.heading: Executive summary
prose: India's data centre market is valued at roughly USD 9.8 billion in 2025, up from about USD 4 billion in 2024 and just USD 1.2 billion in 2021. Installed IT capacity has crossed roughly 1.6-1.9 GW by mid-2026, tripling from around 520 MW in 2020.

Even so, India holds only about 2-5% of global data centre capacity while generating roughly 20% of the world's data, pointing to a long runway for growth. Over USD 120 billion of hyperscaler and conglomerate commitments are backing a build-out toward 6-9 GW by 2029-30.

Growth is being driven by AI workloads, data-localisation rules, new tax and infrastructure-status incentives, and cheaper construction costs than global peers. At the same time, India remains heavily import-dependent for servers, GPUs and power/cooling equipment, and faces grid, water and regulatory constraints that could slow the pace of expansion.

sections.heading: Market size & growth
prose: India's data centre market was valued at USD 9.79 billion in 2025, having grown from USD 4 billion in 2024 and just USD 1.2 billion in 2021. The market is expected to grow at a CAGR of roughly 13.59% through 2031, though different trackers put the range as wide as 13.5-24.6% depending on scope.

Installed IT capacity has tripled from around 520 MW in 2020 to roughly 1.5-1.9 GW by FY26. Multiple trackers project this will reach 4-9+ GW by 2029-30, driven by AI, cloud computing and data-localisation requirements.

sections.heading: Segments
prose: Colocation is the dominant deployment model, capturing 84.45% share in 2025 as enterprises choose to outsource rather than self-build. By value, however, hyperscale facilities account for an estimated 56% of 2026 market value as large self-build campuses from cloud providers scale up.

On the component side, hardware - servers, storage, networking and cooling equipment - dominates with over 55% market share in 2026, valued at more than USD 8.63 billion. By end-use, IT and ITES is the largest vertical at 45.96% of the market, followed by BFSI at 18%, which is also the fastest-growing vertical due to uptime mandates.

Tier 3 facilities, offering N+1 redundancy and 99.98% uptime, are the dominant facility standard, holding 49.15% share in 2025. Geographically, Mumbai and Navi Mumbai dominate with over 52% of installed capacity, followed by Chennai at nearly 20%, which is rising fast due to submarine cable connectivity. At the state level, Maharashtra leads with 26% share.

sections.heading: Value chain
prose: The chain starts with site selection and construction, where hyperscale facilities need 10-50 acres of land. Cost allocation runs roughly 40% to hard costs (land and building), 40% to electrical systems, and 20% to HVAC cooling systems.

Equipment procurement is a critical and import-heavy stage, covering electrical systems, cooling, backup generators, servers and networking gear. Servers alone make up roughly 80% of a data centre's initial setup cost, with equipment sourced from both domestic manufacturers like Netweb and global OEMs such as Dell, HPE and IBM.

Once built, operations and colocation leasing follow, with power making up 65% of operating costs and PUE (power usage effectiveness) ranging from 1.3 in green data centres to 1.9 in conventional ones. On top of the physical layer sits cloud and compute service delivery, dominated by hyperscalers AWS, Azure and Google Cloud, which together hold 87% of India's IaaS market, alongside networking OEMs like Cisco, Juniper and Huawei.

sections.heading: Distribution & channels
prose: Colocation and third-party data centre providers hold nearly 45% of overall data centres in India, as businesses rent space, power and cooling rather than build and operate their own facilities.

Content delivery network (CDN) players operate without a dedicated regulatory or licensing framework in India, making them dependent on telecom service providers for point-to-point connectivity and internet transit.

sections.heading: Key players & positioning
prose: CtrlS, NTT (Netmagic), STT GDC, Sify, Nxtra (Bharti Airtel) and Adani Connex are the top colocation operators, together accounting for a majority of operational capacity. STT GDC runs 70 MW across 2.14 million sq ft with plans to expand to 200 MW. Nxtra has 10 large and 120+ edge data centres nationwide; Carlyle Group bought a 25% stake in Nxtra for USD 235 million.

Yotta Infrastructure operates India's largest single data centre (5.845 MW, Navi Mumbai) and is investing over USD 2 billion to deploy 20,000 Nvidia Blackwell Ultra chips, alongside plans for 100 edge data centres. Adani Group has announced plans to invest up to INR 70,000 crore in solar-powered data parks in Andhra Pradesh, while Hiranandani Group (linked to Yotta) has committed INR 14,000 crore, and Techno Electric & Engineering plans USD 1 billion across major Indian cities.

Global hyperscalers AWS, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud dominate cloud infrastructure with 87% of India's IaaS market. Oracle has launched a Gen 2 Cloud region in Mumbai with another planned in Hyderabad. Google has secured approval for a 600-acre data centre in Vizag via its subsidiary Raiden Infotech India, and Reliance Industries is partnering with Microsoft for SME cloud services.

On hardware, Netweb Technologies is NVIDIA's only Elite OEM partner in India, having installed over 300 supercomputing systems and 4,000+ AI systems. Global OEMs HPE, IBM and Dell maintain extensive India footprints (19, 20 and 8 locations respectively) in servers and storage. Global colocation operator Equinix has announced a USD 15 billion global expansion plan, and NTT has committed USD 1.5 billion to its India expansion.

sections.heading: Margins
prose: EBITDA margins for established India colocation operators have stayed stable at around 40-43% between FY22 and FY25, and can scale toward 50-55% at steady-state utilisation. Power costs are the biggest drag on profitability, making up 65-75% of operating expenses.

Global listed peers Equinix and Digital Realty report comparable EBITDA margins of 37-48%, suggesting India's colocation economics are broadly in line with international benchmarks once scale is reached.

sections.heading: Supply & capacity
prose: The top five to six colocation operators control the majority of India's installed capacity. CtrlS leads with 248 MW across Mumbai, Chennai, Hyderabad and Telangana, followed by STT GDC (202 MW, Mumbai and Chennai-led), NTT (196 MW, Mumbai-led with Bengaluru), Nxtra by Airtel (137 MW, pan-India with 120+ edge sites), Sify (115 MW, Mumbai-Rabale across 12 live facilities), Adani Connex (117 MW, Chennai, Hyderabad, Pune, Vizag) and Yotta (81 MW, Navi Mumbai NM1 campus). The top 5 players account for 66% of total operational capacity.

Capacity utilisation across the industry runs at around 93%, reflecting tight supply relative to demand. India is heavily reliant on imports for high-value components, with about 60% of such equipment imported in 2024; cumulative data centre component imports are projected to reach USD 17 billion between FY26 and FY30.

sections.heading: Tailwinds vs headwinds
prose: Tailwinds include surging AI and hyperscale demand (AI workloads are 5-10x more power-intensive than traditional cloud), data-localisation mandates under the DPDP Act and RBI rules expected to add 1,800-2,000 MW of demand by 2027, and new government incentives including infrastructure status for 5MW+ facilities and a 20-year tax holiday for foreign cloud providers through 2047. The IndiaAI Mission has committed Rs 10,372 crore and onboarded 34,000+ GPUs at subsidised rates of USD 0.76/hr versus USD 3-5/hr internationally. State-level incentives across 15 states, over USD 120 billion in committed investment, and construction costs around USD 7/watt - cheaper than the US (USD 10/W) and UK (USD 11/W) - all support continued buildout.

Headwinds are significant. Regulatory approval processes requiring 40-50 clearances stretch project timelines to 24-30 months versus an achievable 15-18 months elsewhere. Grid transmission and distribution losses of 16.64% are more than double the global average of 6-8%, raising power costs and reliability risk. Major data centre clusters in Maharashtra, Telangana and Tamil Nadu are emerging in states already under severe water stress, with a 100 MW hyperscale facility consuming up to 730 million litres of water annually. India's facilities also remain small by global standards - its largest data centre (5.845 MW) is a fraction of the US average of 20.5 MW - while long lead times of 80-160+ weeks for imported transformers and switchgear risk delaying buildouts. Despite 34,000+ subsidised GPUs available, the national AI Compute Portal had just 144 users as of September 2025, pointing to underutilisation of national compute infrastructure.

sections.heading: Outlook
prose: India's data centre market is set to keep growing fast, from USD 9.79 billion in 2025 at a CAGR of roughly 13.59% through 2031, with installed capacity projected to climb from 1.5-1.9 GW today to 4-9+ GW by 2029-30. This growth is anchored by over USD 120 billion in committed hyperscaler and conglomerate investment, continued AI and cloud demand, data-localisation rules, and supportive government policy including tax holidays and infrastructure status.

The pace of this build-out will depend on how quickly India resolves structural constraints: lengthy regulatory approvals, grid losses well above global norms, water stress in key clusters, undersized facilities relative to global peers, and long import lead times for critical equipment. Addressing these bottlenecks - alongside building out domestic manufacturing in fibre, networking ASICs and transport equipment - will determine whether India can close the gap between its 2-5% share of global capacity and its 20% share of global data generation.
